query: What membership‑inference and privacy validation protocols should be applied to synthetic datasets, and what pass/fail criteria will demonstrate acceptable risk?

response.query: What membership‑inference and privacy validation protocols should be applied to synthetic datasets, and what pass/fail criteria will demonstrate acceptable risk?
response.answer: Membership-inference protocols should use differential privacy tests; pass if synthetic data resists inference of individual membership. Privacy validation should include k-anonymity and differential privacy checks; acceptable risk if metrics meet regulatory standards.

results.title: Label-free Biomedical Imaging and Sensing (LBIS) 2026
results.content: Optical detection methods for label-free imaging and sensing are typically based on internal contrast mechanisms of the sample; for example, its ability to delay the light interacting with the sample due to refractive index changes, or its ability to create unique optical spectroscopic, auto-fluorescence, and birefringence or acoustic signatures. We present dynamic spectrally encoded confocal microscopy (D-SECM), a high-speed, label-free imaging technique for real-time visualization of subcellular metabolic activity. Multispectral imaging (MSI) enables label-free analysis of biological tissues by capturing images across multiple wavelengths, enhancing contrast and biochemical specificity over traditional brightfield microscopy. In contrast, label-free optical imaging enables non-invasive access to phenotypic traits of living cells, keeping them viable and sterile for downstream use. We present a label-free, preparation-free approach to blood-cell imaging based on near-focus interference (NFI) quantitative phase imaging, designed for both pre-clinical and clinical use. Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) based on digital holographic microscopy (DHM), can be combined with microscopes and provides label-free access of biophysical cell properties and morphology.

results.content: Additionally, we utilize the Monte Carlo model of polarized light transfer to model the interaction of the polarized light with optical phantom for both a back-reflected MM and confocal Mueller Matrix imaging to validate our findings. Author(s): Meishu Wang, MOE Key Laboratory of Optoelectronic Imaging Technology and System, Beijing Institute of Technology (China), LPICM, CNRS, Ecole Polytechnique, IP Paris (France); Sooyong Chae, Théotim Lucas, Lab. de Physique des Interfaces et des Couches Minces, CNRS (France), École Polytechnique, Institut Polytechnique de Paris (France); Omar Rodríguez-Núñez, Inselspital (Switzerland); Éléa Romy Gros, Christopher Hahne, Theoni Maragkou, Richard McKinley, Univ. Polarized light is sensitive to the optical anisotropy of white matter, caused by densely packed myelinated fibers, and can enhance contrast in polarimetric images of linear retardance and optical axis azimuth. Our findings bridge structured light optics and biomedical imaging and suggest that OAM-based modalities can complement polarization-sensitive diagnostics.
